claims.text: Some dunes produce sustained low sound during avalanches.
The NPS recording is from Great Sand Dunes National Park.
At Eureka Dunes, dry sand can boom; damp sand does not.
The sound can resemble a low organ note or distant airplane.
Research has proposed different mechanisms for sustaining dune sound.
Relative motion of grains during avalanches is linked to dune sound; synchronization is an influential explanation.
Suitable singing-dune sand produced sound in laboratory avalanches in a hard-bottom channel.
Sorting the mixed-size sand into a narrower grain-size range produced a more defined note.
Field studies proposed layered-dune waveguides, while other experiments emphasize flowing grains.
Sound in air propagates as pressure disturbances while air particles oscillate locally.
Silo studies measured discharge-driven vibration and sound linked to stick-slip wall friction in tall narrow silos.
A flexible bag of granular material can conform to an object and become more rigid under vacuum to grip it.
The 2015 field study distinguished brief burps and sustained booming and reported 70–105 Hz peaks at investigated sites.
Pitch, loudness and spectral concentration are different sound properties.
These examples connect through granular physics; direct derivation from dune-acoustics research is not established.
